edits.anchor: We modelled the sleep-wake behavioral sequence
Hidden Markov model of sleep-wake dynamics

paras.text: Each fly's behaviour was represented on a 1-minute grid by three observable symbols: sleep (S), quiet wake (Q) and active wake (W). The primary description is the observed first-order Markov chain on these symbols, with phase-specific transition matrices (Observed S/Q/W chain, below); all reported directions of circulation, cycle fluxes, entropy production rates, Onsager conductances and state energies are computed from it, per fly and phase. A three-state discrete-time hidden Markov model (HMM) with the same structure was fitted as well. Its hidden states emit the symbols nearly one-to-one (median P(Q | H_{1}) 0.80–0.94, P(W | H_{2}) 0.91–0.96, P(S | H_{3}) ≈ 1), so it adds a model of misclassification and short-range structure rather than new states; it is used as a robustness check, and its thermodynamic quantities as a model-based estimate, not as a bound (Observable and hidden levels compared, below). The quiet-wake symbol is needed for either description: with a binary sleep/wake observable the intermediate state has no emission signature of its own; in most 4-hour windows its emission row coincided with that of the wake or the sleep state, and transition matrices of identical likelihood then span essentially the full range of the routing and thermodynamic quantities defined below, a known property of aggregated Markov models (Fredkin & Rice, 1986; Kienker, 1989).

Sleep was scored from the 1-s locomotor counts as inactivity lasting ≥ 5 min. A single active second was bridged (set to inactive) only when the inactive runs on both sides each lasted ≥ 5 min, measured on the unbridged trace. A minute was labelled S if at least 30 of its 60 s fell within a sleep bout. Each remaining (wake) minute was labelled Q if its fraction of active seconds was below θ r_{f}, and W otherwise. The reference r_{f} is the fly's typical wake activity: the median, over that fly's wake bouts lasting ≥ 10 min, of the fraction of active seconds (count > 0) in the bout's central 5 min. It was computed separately for the light and dark phases, a bout contributing to a phase if its waking or its sleep onset fell in that phase, and over the whole record in constant darkness; at least 3 such bouts were required, otherwise the wake minutes of that phase were treated as missing (emission likelihood 1). Scaling the threshold to each fly's own wake activity makes 'quiet' a relative state, so that differences in overall activity between flies and genotypes do not by themselves decide the Q/W split. We used θ = 0.5, a value chosen after inspection of the transition-aligned activity profiles, and report θ = 0.33 and 0.75 as sensitivity analyses; every circulation direction that was significant at θ = 0.5 had the same sign at all three values (only near-zero, non-significant blocks changed sign). Recordings were truncated to whole days.
Observed S/Q/W chain

For each fly, the probability of each symbol change was estimated separately for transitions into minutes at ZT 0–12 and at ZT 12–24 (a single matrix in constant darkness; for CS also four 6-hour blocks) by maximum likelihood. Minutes without a classification were marginalized exactly with the forward algorithm (the chain is the HMM below with the identity as emission matrix); on complete records the estimate equals the normalized transition counts. Q, W and S take the indices 1, 2 and 3 of the hidden states H_{1}, H_{2} and H_{3}, so that every quantity defined below for the hidden level applies unchanged to the observed chain. The direction of circulation was measured by the minute-level observable current *c*_{obs} = P(Q | last wake minute before a sleep onset) − P(Q | first wake minute after a waking); the cycle flux *J*_{cycle} (Eq. 20) and the entropy production (Eq. 22, rule-of-three bound) from the directed symbol-change counts; and the cycle affinity (Eq. 21), the stationary entropy production and the state energies (Eqs. 5 and 7) from the fitted transition matrices. Count-based and matrix-based fluxes agreed per fly (Spearman correlation 0.98–1.00 in every genotype and phase). Fly–phases without a Q/W reference were excluded, and fly–phases whose fitted chain carries no net cycle current (|*J*| < 10^{-12}) were excluded from directional and thermodynamic summaries. These are of three kinds, counted separately: exactly symmetric transition counts (a cycle with zero current), a transition never observed in either direction (its rate only bounded), and a state absent from the phase. Medians of the chain entropy production rank infinite values (a transition observed in one direction only) highest rather than dropping them. Group values are medians over flies with 95% intervals from a bootstrap over flies (2000 resamples). Where many flies carry no qualifying transitions in a phase, so that the median is zero (*sss*), the group mean with a bootstrap 95% interval is reported beside the median, and the sign of the observed-chain flux was tested by a Wilcoxon signed-rank test over the flies whose chain carries a cycle (fly–phases with |*J*| < 10^{-12} have no cycle; they are counted and set to zero, never assigned a sign).
Hidden Markov model: robustness check and model-based estimate

The hidden Markov model was fitted for three reasons. First, the symbols are scored rather than observed, so a minute near the quiet/active threshold can be misclassified; a model with an explicit emission matrix asks whether a result survives once misclassification is allowed for. Second, coarse-graining can only lower entropy production (Esposito, 2012), so dissipation measured on the observed symbols is a lower bound, and hidden states could carry dissipation that the observed chain does not show. Third, fly sleep has internal structure, including deeper stages within long bouts (van Alphen et al., 2013; Tainton-Heap et al., 2021) and processes visible only in transition probabilities (Wiggin et al., 2020); a hidden-state model asks whether behaviour alone reveals such states. The model was used as a check on results that could otherwise be artefacts of scoring, and its quantities are reported as model-based estimates, not as bounds.

The HMM has *K* hidden states, a *K* × 3 emission matrix *B* shared by all times of day, an initial distribution *π*_{0}, and phase-specific transition matrices: *P*^{L} for transitions into minutes at ZT 0–12 and *P*^{D} for transitions into minutes at ZT 12–24 (a single matrix *P* in constant darkness). Within each phase the dynamics are assumed time-homogeneous. One model was fitted per fly to its entire recording by maximum likelihood, using Baum–Welch expectation–maximization in which the expected transition counts are accumulated separately by the phase of the arrival minute and the emission counts are pooled. Each fit was started from 20 random initializations (half with diagonally dominant transition matrices) and iterated until the relative gain in log-likelihood fell below 10^{-7} for every initialization, or for at most 1000 iterations; the best final likelihood was retained.

Models with *K* = 2, 3 and 4 were fitted, and the order was selected by the Bayesian information criterion, BIC = −2*LL* + *k* ln *n*, with *k* = (*K* − 1) + *n*_{P}*K*(*K* − 1) + 2*K* free parameters (*n*_{P} = 2 phases) and *n* the number of minutes; as a sensitivity analysis *n* was replaced by the number of symbol changes. A fly was flagged, not excluded, when *K* = 2 or 4 improved BIC over *K* = 3 by more than 10. Routing and thermodynamic quantities are defined for *K* = 3. The three states were labelled by their emissions: H_{3} has the largest P(S | H), H_{2} the larger P(W | H) of the remaining two, and H_{1} is the third. H_{1} was considered unidentified in a fly if its emission row lay within total-variation distance 0.05 of the row of H_{2} or H_{3}; such flies were excluded from routing and thermodynamic summaries and counted. BIC selected *K* = 3 in 76–96% of flies of each genotype (with *n* the number of symbol changes, 56–91%; under this lighter penalty 40% of *per0* (DD) and 26% of *fumin* flies preferred *K* = 4), and *K* = 3 was used throughout. No hidden Markov models were fitted to CS in constant darkness. Whether the *K* = 3 model improves on the observed chain is a separate comparison (Observable and hidden levels compared, below).

Single 4-hour windows were not fitted separately, because one window does not contain enough sleep–wake transitions to resolve routing: on synthetic sequences with a distinct H_{1} and known routing, a single 240-minute window selected *K* = 3 in only 4% of cases and gave routing fractions with a standard deviation of 0.75 (Validation of the inference, below). As a secondary design with finer time resolution, CS, *per0* (LD) and *fumin* flies were also fitted with four transition matrices, one for each 6-hour block (ZT 0–6, 6–12, 12–18, 18–24), with shared emissions.
Model-free cycle current

To obtain a direction of circulation that does not depend on any HMM, each sleep onset and each waking was classified directly from the 1-s counts. For every wake bout lasting ≥ 10 min between two sleep bouts, the active fraction in seconds 61–300 after the waking (exit) and in seconds 61–300 before the next sleep onset (approach) was labelled Q if below θ r_{f} and A (active) otherwise, with r_{f} as defined above for the phase of the transition; the first minute next to each transition was excluded because it contains a movement by definition. The model-free current is *c* = P(Q | onset) − P(Q | waking), computed per fly and light phase. Positive *c* indicates the forward cycle A → Q → S → A, which corresponds to H_{2} → H_{1} → H_{3} → H_{2}, i.e. the forward direction of *J*_{cycle} defined below.
Round trips around sleep bouts

Each sleep bout was classified by its entry and exit route into one of four round-trip types: forward (quiet entry, active exit; Q → S → A), reverse (A → S → Q), direct (A → S → A) and quiet on both sides (Q → S → Q). At the level of observed behaviour, sleep bouts flanked on both sides by wake bouts lasting ≥ 10 min were used, entry and exit being classified as in the model-free cycle current, with r_{f} of the phase of the sleep onset. At the hidden level, the same four types were counted on each posterior path for visits to H_{3} lasting ≥ 5 min that were preceded and followed by ≥ 10 min without H_{3} (the definition matched to the behavioural one), with H_{1} in the role of Q and H_{2} in the role of A; fractions were computed per path and averaged over paths. A round trip was assigned to the phase of its sleep onset; flies needed at least 3 round trips in a phase. For each fly and phase we report the fraction and the rate per hour of each type, the marginal probabilities of a quiet entry and a quiet exit, and the difference between each type's fraction and the product of the marginals (a test of whether entry and exit routes are independent). Forward and reverse fractions were compared within flies by Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, Holm-corrected over genotype–phase blocks.
Dependence of routing on bout duration

To test whether the choice of route depends on the history of the bout, three relations were examined for each sleep bout: R1, whether the exit was quiet (Q, or H_{1} at the hidden level) or active (A, or H_{2}) against the duration of the sleep bout it ended; R2, whether the entry was quiet or active against the duration of the preceding wake period; and R3, the entry route against the duration of the sleep bout it began. In a Markov model the exit route from a state is independent of the time spent in it, so a dependence in R1 is a direct departure from the Markov description. At the level of observed behaviour, sleep bouts (bridged scoring) were used; an exit was classified only if the following wake bout lasted ≥ 10 min and an entry only if the preceding one did, by comparing the active fraction in seconds 61–300 after waking (before onset) with θ r_{f} as in the model-free cycle current. At the hidden level, visits to H_{3} lasting ≥ 5 min with a previous and a next visit were used on each of 200 posterior paths, an entry (exit) being classified when the gap since the previous (until the next) H_{3} visit was ≥ 10 min, the neighbouring state giving the route. A bout was assigned to the light phase of its onset. The null permuted route labels among each fly's bouts within phase (2000 permutations); because a Holm-corrected threshold near *p* = 0.006 lies within the Monte Carlo error of 2000 permutations, the one borderline block (*per0* (LD), light) was checked with 20,000 permutations (*p* = 0.004). In figures, the memoryless reference is each group's overall probability of a quiet exit, which a Markov chain predicts at every bout length.

For each fly and phase, the effect was summarised as *D* = ⟨ln *t*⟩_{quiet} − ⟨ln *t*⟩_{active}, the difference between the mean log durations of bouts with a quiet and with an active route, requiring at least two bouts of each kind; *D* < 0 means that quiet routes go with shorter bouts. At the hidden level *D* was computed on each posterior path and averaged over the paths on which it was defined (at least half). The group statistic was the mean of *D* over flies. At the observed level its null distribution was obtained by permuting the route labels among each fly's own bouts within the phase (2000 permutations), which preserves each fly's durations and route frequencies and removes only their association; because the comparison is made within flies, differences between flies cannot produce an effect. At the hidden level the null was obtained from 400 records simulated from each fly's fitted model and decoded with the same procedure, which gives the value expected from a Markov process through the full pipeline. Two-sided p-values were Holm-corrected over genotype–phase blocks, separately for each relation and level. For illustration, the probability of a quiet route was also plotted in fixed duration bins (sleep 5–10, 10–20, 20–40, 40–80, > 80 min; wake 10–20, 20–40, 40–80, 80–160, > 160 min), weighting flies equally and showing only bins to which at least 10 flies contributed; these binned curves are descriptive.

edits.anchor: We define the routing fraction as the proportion
We define the routing fraction as the proportion

paras.text: We define the routing fraction as the proportion of Sleep→Wake transitions that travel via the indirect path (H_{3} → H_{1} → H_{2}) rather than the direct path (H_{3} → H_{2}), and analogously for Wake→Sleep. Route counts were obtained from the posterior distribution of hidden paths rather than from the single most probable (Viterbi) path, because a functional of the most probable path is a biased estimator of the posterior expectation of that functional. For each fly, 200 hidden paths spanning the whole recording were drawn under the fitted model by forward filtering–backward sampling, so no window boundaries enter the counting. Each sampled path was run-length compressed, and the direct and indirect Sleep→Wake counts (*N*_{32}, *N*_{312}) and Wake→Sleep counts (*N*_{23}, *N*_{213}) were obtained by matching the corresponding two- or three-entry patterns, which requires the matched trajectory to begin and end at Sleep/Wake (or Wake/Sleep) with no other intervening state. Each route was assigned to the light phase (or 6-hour block) of the minute in which it completes. The directed single-step counts *N*_{ij} used below were taken from the same compressed paths.

Every nonlinear function of the counts (the routing fractions, Eqs. 14–15, and the entropy production, Eq. 22) was evaluated on each sampled path and then averaged over the 200 paths, respecting Jensen's inequality. On a given path a routing fraction required at least 3 routes in its denominator; a fly's value was reported if it was defined on at least half of its paths. Viterbi counts were computed for comparison only. In the S/Q/W analysis the model-predicted routing fractions (Eq. 16) were computed from the phase matrices *P*^{L} and *P*^{D} rather than per window.

By the flow-balance identity that follows

paras.text: In the S/Q/W analysis, *N*_{32} and *N*_{23} (S→W and W→S symbol changes) were counted on the observed symbols, by the phase of the arrival minute, and divided by the number of recorded hours in the phase (or block), *T*_{phase}. The stationary flux of the fitted chain, *J* = π_{2}*P*(2,1) − π_{1}*P*(1,2) per step, converted to transitions per hour, agreed with the count-based value (per-fly Spearman correlation 0.98–1.00 in every genotype and phase). For the HMM-based estimate, the same counts were taken on each of 200 posterior paths; because *J*_{cycle} is linear in the counts, its posterior mean equals Eq. (20) evaluated on the posterior-mean counts. For a three-state chain, the sign of *J*_{cycle} equals the sign of the cycle affinity (Eq. 21) and of the routing difference (*F*_{W→S} − *F*_{S→W})/2 computed from the same matrix, so all three report the same direction of circulation. A phase in which one edge of the cycle was numerically absent (|*J*| < 10^{-12}) carries no cycle and was excluded from directional analyses.

edits.anchor: where  is the total count of  transitions

paras.text: In the S/Q/W analysis, Eq. (22) was evaluated on the observed symbol-change counts, with *T*_{phase} in place of *T*_{valid} (for the HMM-based estimate, on each posterior path and then averaged over paths). The observability gate was replaced by a bound. An edge pair traversed in one direction only (count *k* in one direction, 0 in the other) states that the reverse rate is below the detection limit; at 95% confidence that limit is 3 transitions over the recording (the Poisson zero-count limit, or rule of three). The edge term (*k* − *b*) ln(*k*/*b*) decreases monotonically in the unobserved count *b* and vanishes at *b* = *k*, so its minimum over the permitted range 0 ≤ *b* ≤ 3 lies at *b*^{∗} = min(3, *k*). The term therefore becomes (*k* − 3) ln(*k*/3) for *k* > 3 and 0 otherwise. Substituting *b*^{∗} in both the prefactor and the logarithm makes each such edge term a 95% lower bound given the observed forward count, and the sum non-negative by construction; it coincides with Eq. (22) whenever both directions are observed. The estimator as a whole is not a lower bound on the true rate: with finite counts the Schnakenberg sum is biased upward when the true irreversibility is small (Validation of the inference, item vii). Model-based entropy production per phase was computed from the fitted transition matrix at its stationary distribution, and was reported as infinite when a transition was present in one direction only.

edits.anchor: Onsager linear response and thermodynamic conductance

paras.text: Validation of the inference

Every inference step was tested on synthetic data before it was applied to flies, with pass criteria fixed in advance. (i) Positive control: 20 synthetic flies (4 days each) were generated from a three-state model with a distinct H_{1} emission and known phase-specific routing (light *F*_{S→W} = −0.3, *F*_{W→S} = +0.4; dark +0.2 and −0.1) and refitted. BIC selected *K* = 3 in all flies, and the routing fractions were recovered with bias ≤ 0.03 and standard deviation 0.20–0.27. (ii) Negative controls: two-state truths without H_{1}, with and without a factor-of-two drift of the exit rates across each 12-hour phase, selected *K* = 2 in all flies, so neither a missing state nor within-phase drift was mistaken for H_{1}. (iii) Reversible null: a three-state truth obeying detailed balance in both phases gave fitted cycle currents of zero within ±0.03, so the procedure does not create circulation; the fitted entropy production of such reversible flies reached 0.26–0.33 nats h^{-1} (95th percentile), which we take as the noise floor for single-fly values.

(iv) Per-fly precision: for 5 flies per genotype, 30 records simulated from each fly's fitted model were refitted (parametric bootstrap), giving the standard deviation of single-fly routing fractions. (v) Posterior-predictive checks: records simulated from each fly's fitted model were compared with the data, both for the fractions of S, Q and W minutes and the number of symbol changes in every 4-hour window, and for the observable current *c*_{obs} = P(Q | last wake minute before a sleep onset) − P(Q | first wake minute after a waking). The latter also gives the expected ratio between the hidden current and the observable current under coarse-graining. (vi) For the 6-hour design, 20 records simulated from each of 5 flies' fitted models per genotype were refitted with the 6-hour model; the design was deemed usable for a genotype if the median standard deviation of its routing fractions was below 0.3 in every block, which held for CS and *per0* (LD) but not for *fumin*. (vii) Entropy-production estimators: for every fly, 20 records simulated from its fitted model were analysed with the count-based estimators at the hidden level (posterior paths decoded with the true parameters) and at the observable level (S/Q/W symbols), and compared with the model's exact stationary entropy production. For flies whose fitted model has every transition in both directions, the hidden estimator exceeded the exact value by a roughly constant +0.01 to +0.025 nats h^{-1}, negligible where circulation is strong but comparable to the value itself where it is weak. For flies whose fitted model has a transition in one direction only (17–36% of *fumin* and *sss* flies), the exact value is infinite or very large while the count estimator remains small. Entropy production and the hidden–observable difference were therefore interpreted only in phases with substantial circulation. (viii) Time resolution: for CS and *fumin* (78 flies), symbols were rebuilt on a 30-s grid by the same rules (S if at least 15 s of the bin lay in a sleep bout; otherwise Q or W from the bin's active fraction against the same θ*r*_{f}), and the three-state model was refitted with 20 starts. No fly had a degenerate H_{1} at either resolution. The median H_{1} mean dwell time fell from 2.5–3.5 min to 1.8–2.3 min (ratio of medians 0.56–0.73; paired Wilcoxon *p* < 10^{−6} in every genotype–phase block), and at 30 s only 21–27% of decoded H_{1} runs lasted a single step, so H_{1} is a state of about 2 min that the 1-min grid partly truncates; part of the shortening may reflect Q/W flicker, because each 30-s symbol rests on half as much activity data. In contrast, *J*_{cycle} and entropy production did not change significantly in any block except *fumin* in the light (*J*_{cycle} +22%, *p* = 0.04). The direction of circulation per fly kept its sign in 76–92% of fly–phases (lowest in CS in the light, where circulation is near zero), and the dependence of exit route on sleep-bout length in CS at night persisted (hidden-level *D* = −0.19 at 30 s, 80% of flies negative, Wilcoxon *p* = 0.006, against −0.28 at 1 min). The 1-min grid was therefore retained for all analyses.
Changes in the direction of circulation

For the 6-hour design, the per-fly routing difference *c*_{b} = (*F*_{W→S} − *F*_{S→W})/2 in block *b*, whose sign is the direction of *J*_{cycle}, was tested against zero in each block by a one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test (Holm-corrected over the four blocks). Change across the day was tested by a Friedman test over the four blocks, followed by Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on within-fly differences between adjacent blocks (Holm-corrected). A change of direction was claimed only if two blocks had significant group directions of opposite sign that also differed significantly within flies. Changes across days were assessed by refitting the first and second halves of each fly's recording separately. Whether more flies changed sign than expected from estimation noise alone was tested against each fly's sign-flip probability under a no-change null: 8 records were simulated from the fly's whole-record model, split and refitted in the same way, and the observed number of flips was compared with the resulting Poisson-binomial distribution. The same no-change simulations, analysed with the within-phase Wilcoxon tests, were used to verify that the 6-hour estimator does not by itself create differences between blocks.
Observable and hidden levels compared

To ask whether the hidden layer is needed, the HMM was compared per fly with the observed first-order chain, which is the same model with the emission matrix fixed to the identity (*k* = 20 and 14 free parameters). The HMM's gain in log-likelihood was small (median 9–18 nats per fly, ≈ 3 nats per 1000 minutes), and BIC preferred the observed chain in 72–77% of CS and *fumin* flies. Because this comparison lies on a boundary of the parameter space, its significance was assessed by a parametric bootstrap (10 records simulated from each of 20 flies' fitted chains and refitted with both models): the chain was rejected in 16 of the 20 flies. In predictive simulations the chain reproduced switching rates, run lengths and the observable current at least as well as the HMM. A second-order chain matched 1.25–2 times the HMM's likelihood gain, whereas allowing four 6-hour transition matrices removed almost none of it; the HMM therefore captures short-range structure around single-minute switches rather than slow drift. Whether that structure is misclassification or genuine short memory cannot be separated with these models.

Whether this short-range structure carries additional irreversibility was tested with the Kullback–Leibler divergence rate between the symbol sequence and its time reverse, estimated from blocks of *n* = 2, 3 and 4 minutes (Roldán & Parrondo, 2010) with a pseudocount of 0.5 per block. For a stationary first-order chain the increment *d*_{n} = *D*_{n} − *D*_{n−1} does not depend on *n*, so the excess *E* of *d*_{3} − *d*_{2} over its value in 200 records simulated from each fly's own chain (same length, phases and missing minutes) measures irreversibility carried by memory beyond one minute. A genotype × phase block was considered to show it if *E* was positive by a Wilcoxon test (Holm correction over 10 blocks), more flies than expected by chance had individual *p* < 0.05, and both held against a second null with 6-hour transition matrices. This was met in *per0* (DD) (*E* = +0.06 nats h^{-1}, also in sequences without sleep) and in *fumin* in the dark (+0.04 nats h^{-1}, confined to sequences containing sleep, where the 5-minute sleep criterion could contribute), and in no other block, including CS in light–dark cycles and CS in constant darkness analysed in 12-hour halves.

The thermodynamic uncertainty relation, σ ≥ *J*^{2}/*D* for any current of a Markov jump process in a steady state, with *D* = Var[*N*(*t*)]/2*t* (Barato & Seifert, 2015), was applied per fly to the net count *N*(*t*) of forward symbol changes (W→Q, Q→S and S→W counted +1, their reverses −1). *D* was estimated from the variance of *N* over non-overlapping 3-hour blocks (2- and 6-hour blocks as sensitivity analyses), the bias of this estimator was calibrated with 200 records simulated from the fly's own chain, and the small excess over the continuous-time bound that 1-minute sampling permits (≤ 0.5% for the fitted chains) was removed. The fitted chains themselves lie close to the bound (median ratio of bound to entropy production 0.90–1.00), as expected for a single cycle near equilibrium; this is a property of the model, not a finding. In constant darkness, the steady-state case, the ratio for the data was 0.90 in *per0* and 0.75 in CS, and no fly exceeded its own simulated null; in light–dark cycles, where periodic driving permits violations and the comparison is descriptive, the ratios were 0.51–0.95. Including fly–phases with a transition observed in one direction only, with the rule-of-three substitution, gave 0.73–0.84 in the affected blocks. The relation therefore indicates no dissipation beyond that of the observed chain.

HMM-based values are reported beside the observable ones as a model-based estimate, not as a bound. Per fly, the HMM's cycle flux was about 1.0–1.2 times and its count-based entropy production 1.2–3.6 times the observable value (medians by genotype and phase), but its model entropy production was below that of the observed chain in the light phase of CS, *fumin* and *sss*, and the HMM's entropy production reached the triplet-based lower bound above in only 44–73% of fly–phases. All observable–hidden comparisons were made within fly and phase.

Waiting-time irreversibility. In a first-order chain the time spent in a state does not depend on the states before and after it. For runs of Q and of W whose neighbouring minutes were classified, the dwell-time distributions for the two directions of passage, W→Q→S against S→Q→W and Q→W→S against S→W→Q (bins of 1, 2, 3, 4–5, 6–9 and ≥ 10 min; pseudocount 0.5 per bin), were compared by the Kullback–Leibler divergence, weighted by the rate of such runs, giving σ_{WT} in nats h^{-1} (Martínez et al., 2019; van der Meer et al., 2022; Harunari et al., 2022). The excess *E*_{WT} of σ_{WT} over its median in 200 records simulated from each fly's own chain was tested in constant darkness as for *E* above (Wilcoxon test with Holm correction over the blocks, and more flies than expected by chance with individual *p* < 0.05); light–dark blocks were analysed descriptively, with 12-hour and 6-hour chain nulls. Every condition contains an entry into or an exit from sleep, which is scored by the 5-minute criterion. The scoring is, however, exactly time-symmetric on these data: scoring the time-reversed 1-s record gave the time-reversed symbol sequence in every minute (0 of 275,040 minutes differed, *per0* and CS in constant darkness). For a stationary, time-reversible activity process, a time-symmetric scoring yields a reversible symbol process, in which both directions of passage have the same dwell distribution, so the sleep criterion cannot by itself produce an excess. A direct control, σ_{WT} of time-reversible hidden Markov models of each fly's 1-s activity (Wake-bout hazard and its controls) scored identically and matched in run counts, was pre-specified; it could not be evaluated: in neither *per0* (DD) nor CS (DD) did a reversible model with up to six hidden states reproduce the bout process (simulated wake bouts exceeded the observed number by a median of 22% and 40%), so no scoring-matched verdict exists. To show where the dependence lies, the survival curves of the two directions were plotted, without a test, for CS in the dark phase, the light–dark block with the largest excess (fly bootstrap, 1000 resamples).

Activity at the two ends of wake bouts. For each wake bout of at least 600 s between two sleep bouts, the active fraction (count > 0) was computed in 10-s bins over the first 300 s after waking and, time-reversed, over the last 300 s before sleep onset (secondary setting: 120 s in 5-s bins). Each bout's difference profile was centred on its own mean, removing the difference in level, and the statistic was the sum over bins of the squared mean centred difference. Because the scoring is exactly time-symmetric, the two ends of a bout are exchangeable for a stationary, time-reversible activity process; the null flipped the sign of each bout's difference (2000 random flips), with two sensitivity nulls that flipped all bouts of a day together, within fly and across flies. A genotype showed a shape asymmetry if the group Wilcoxon test of the per-fly standardized statistic was positive (Holm over *per0* (DD) and CS (DD)) under all nulls. Traces simulated from a time-reversible model of the 1-s activity gave no positive. This analysis confirms the direction of the observed cycle in the raw 1-s counts, independent of the minute grid and of the quiet/active threshold; it does not measure irreversibility beyond the observed chain, which itself predicts such an asymmetry.
Circadian modulation of the cycle

For each genotype, symbol changes were pooled over flies and days in twelve 2-hour bins of clock time (ZT in light–dark cycles; time from the start of each day of the analysed record in constant darkness), and the cycle flux was computed per bin from the pooled counts. A first harmonic, *J*(*b*) = *m* + *a* cos(2π*b*/12) + *c* sin(2π*b*/12), was fitted by least squares; its amplitude *A* = (*a*^{2} + *c*^{2})^{1/2} was the test statistic, and its phase is reported descriptively. The null distribution came from 999 replicates in which each fly's whole-day record was rotated circularly by an independent random offset, uniform over 24 h in whole minutes, with no transition counted across the junction, and then passed through the identical pooling and fit. The rotation keeps each fly's own rhythm, noise and sample size and destroys only the phase shared across flies; *p* = (1 + #{*A** ≥ *A*})/1000. Holm correction was applied over CS (LD), CS (DD) and *per0* (LD); *per0* (DD) was the negative control. On 200 datasets simulated from constant-rate chains matched to *per0* (DD), the test gave *p* < 0.05 in 4.5% of cases. *c*_{obs} was analysed in the same way as a secondary readout. In constant darkness, differences in free-running period between flies spread the phase by up to about 2 h over the record, so the amplitude is a lower estimate. A first pre-specified summary, the range of the twelve bins with a bootstrap over flies, was found to have no power (its 95% band lay above the point estimate even in *per0* (DD)); it is reported as such and not used for inference.

In the S/Q/W analysis, entropy production and cycle flux were related per fly and light phase rather than per genotype mean. Each point is one fly in one phase: *J*_{cycle} is the count-based flux of the observed symbols (Eq. 20) and EPR the rule-of-three bound (Entropy production rate) from the same counts. Fly–phases with no cycle (|*J*| < 10^{-12}) or without a Q/W reference were excluded. For each genotype, light and dark phases pooled, two descriptions were compared by least squares with a free intercept *b*: constant cycle affinity, EPR = *b* + *a*|*J*_{cycle}|, with *a* the typical affinity in nats per cycle; and linear response, EPR = *b* + *J*_{cycle}^{2}/*L*. The free intercept absorbs any additive offset of the count estimator (calibrated at ≈ 0.01–0.025 nats h^{-1} for the posterior-path estimator, Validation item vii) and is not given a physical interpretation. Both descriptions have two parameters and were compared by their residual sums of squares. The exponent *n* of EPR ∝ |*J*_{cycle}|^{n} was estimated as the slope of ln(EPR − 0.02) on ln|*J*_{cycle}| over points with |*J*_{cycle}| ≥ 0.05 cycles h^{-1} and EPR ≥ 0.05 nats h^{-1}; *n* ≈ 1 indicates constant affinity and *n* ≈ 2 linear response.

The Onsager conductance was then estimated as in Eq. (25), by ordinary least squares of EPR on *J*_{cycle}^{2} through the origin, per genotype, both pooled over phases and per phase, with *L* = 1/slope, its standard error by error propagation and its 95% interval by inverting the interval of the slope. Because the light and dark points of a fly are not independent, intervals were also obtained by a bootstrap over flies (2000 resamples, each fly's phases kept together), and genotypes were compared with the control by the bootstrap distribution of the difference in *L*; the five comparisons with the control were corrected by the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. The Wald test on the slope overstates significance: in a calibration with 400 simulated pairs of genotypes of equal *L* and entropy-proportional noise, it rejected at nominal 5% in 22% of replicates, against 5.2% for the bootstrap difference. Fitting with a free intercept instead of through the origin changed the slope by 0–11% (largest in *fumin*), and using the exact flux and entropy production of the fitted chains instead of the counts changed *L* by at most 0.011; neither changed the ordering of CS, *per0* (LD, DD), *fumin* and *sss*. HMM-based values of *L* (Validation of the inference) are reported for comparison only. For a single edge with one-way traffic *N* (transitions h^{-1}) and net current *J*, the Schnakenberg term is *J* ln[(*N* + *J*/2)/(*N* − *J*/2)] ≈ *J*^{2}/*N* when *J* ≪ *N*; a quadratic relation between EPR and *J*_{cycle} therefore indicates net currents that are small relative to the back-and-forth traffic on each edge, even when the summed cycle affinity is of order one nat per cycle.

edits.anchor: Hidden Markov model of sleep-wake dynamics

paras.text: Wake-bout hazard and its controls

Sleep and wake bouts were extracted from the 1-s counts with the laboratory pipeline (5-min sleep criterion, single active seconds bridged as described above, bouts touching the start or end of the record dropped). In constant darkness, after removal of the first 24 h of each record, this gave 4017 wake bouts from 25 *per0* flies and 3309 from 25 CS flies. The hazard of ending a wake bout was estimated as a life table on logarithmically spaced bins, discarding bins with fewer than 10 bouts at risk. The number of bins was fixed in advance at 12, 16, 20 and 24, and all four are reported, because the outcome depends on it. A rise of the hazard after a trough was summarized by the ratio of the largest hazard after the minimum to the minimum (RiseRatio). Its significance (RiseNullP) was obtained from 999 datasets of the observed size simulated from a two-exponential mixture fitted by maximum likelihood to the same bouts (left-truncated at 2 s, discrete in 1-s bins), whose hazard is strictly decreasing; each simulated dataset was passed through the whole estimator, including the choice of its own bin edges. The power to detect a rise of the size seen in *per0* at the sample sizes of CS was estimated by simulation.

Two controls asked whether a rise could be produced by the scoring rule acting on time-reversible activity. A scored wake bout ends at a silence that later reaches 5 min; it is therefore not a sojourn of the underlying activity process, and the monotone hazard of sojourns in reversible Markov chains (Keilson, 1979) does not apply to it, so any such comparison has to pass through the scoring. (i) Renewal null: each fly's record was rebuilt from independent alternating runs of active and inactive seconds drawn from that fly's own run lengths, a statistically time-reversible process, and scored with the identical pipeline. (ii) Reversible hidden Markov null: each fly's 1-s active/inactive sequence was fitted with an aggregated hidden Markov model with 1–3 active and 1–3 inactive hidden states, deterministic emissions and a transition matrix reversible by construction (*P*_{ij} = *F*_{ij}/π_{i} with *F* symmetric), estimated by expectation–maximization with the reversible maximum-likelihood update (Bowman et al., 2009), 10 random starts per order and the order chosen by BIC. Before use, the model had to reproduce the bout process: the median ratio, over flies, of simulated to observed wake-bout count and of total sleep had to lie within [0.85, 1.15], from 20 simulated records per fly. A control was evaluated only if it passed, with RiseNullP replaced by the fraction of 199 pooled null datasets, subsampled to the observed number of bouts, whose RiseRatio reached the observed one.

edits.anchor: Homeostatic response of HMM parameters to sleep deprivation
To identify which hidden state’s parameters respond

paras.text: Sleep deprivation: within-fly contrasts with a day-to-day control

CS males (*n* = 26) were recorded for 9.5 days, and the sleep deprivator (above) ran during ZT 15–24 of the fourth day, after three baseline days. Symbols were assigned as above, except that each fly's wake reference *r*_{f} was computed from the three baseline days only and applied to all days, so that a change in activity after deprivation could not move the Q/W threshold. The deprivation night itself was excluded. Readouts were computed in the first 6 h of recovery (ZT 0–6 of the following day, a window chosen before the recordings were analysed) and compared within fly with the same window on the baseline days, pooled. There was no undeprived control group, so day-to-day variation was estimated in the same flies by a placebo contrast of identical form, day 3 against days 1–2 of the baseline. A readout (*c*_{obs}, *J*_{cycle} and entropy production; Holm correction over the three) was considered changed only if its change differed from zero by a Wilcoxon signed-rank test and also differed from the placebo change by a paired Wilcoxon test, in the same direction. The rebound itself was assessed as the change in sleep in the same window. Changes in the six transition probabilities were estimated from group-pooled chains with a bootstrap over flies (2000 resamples) and, as a post hoc analysis, contrasted with the placebo ratio computed on the same resampled flies (Holm correction over six); the median active fraction of wake minutes was compared in the same way (post hoc). Association with the amount of sleep lost was assessed by Spearman correlation, in all flies and in flies awake for at least 80% of the deprivation window.
Silencing of dorsal fan-shaped body and ventral nerve cord neurons

UAS-Kir2.1 was expressed constitutively under a dFB split-GAL4 (*n* = 25), a VNC split-GAL4 (*n* = 34) or an enhancerless GAL4 (*n* = 19, control), all in one common genetic background that was not backcrossed to CS. Males were recorded in one run, in one incubator, in 12 h:12 h light–dark cycles, on three monitors; each record starts at ZT 0 and was analysed over 8 whole days. Silenced groups were compared only with the enhancerless-GAL4 control, never with the other genotypes of this study. The control carries a complete GAL4 whereas the drivers are split-GAL4s; an empty split-GAL4 control was not available. Symbols, observed chains and all observable quantities were computed exactly as above (θ = 0.5, light and dark phases). Per-fly values were compared between groups by two-sided Mann–Whitney tests, with the probability of superiority and the difference of group medians (bootstrap over flies, 2000 resamples) as effect sizes. Sleep per phase served as a positive control (Holm correction over 4 tests). The primary family was *c*_{obs}, *J*_{cycle} and the count-based entropy production in each phase and for each driver (Holm over 12); the six transition probabilities (Holm over 24), the state energies (Holm over 8) and the Onsager conductance (bootstrap over flies) were secondary. Monitor effects were checked within genotype (VNC flies on two monitors, control flies on two monitors), and the primary family was recomputed without the first day as a sensitivity analysis.

The dependence of the exit route from sleep on the length of the sleep bout (Dependence of routing on bout duration) was compared between groups per fly by Mann–Whitney tests (Holm over 4). A pre-specified comparison of the sleep-bout duration distributions between groups (time constant and observed weight of the slow component of a two-exponential mixture) was withdrawn before it was run, because silenced flies already left sleep sooner and the comparison would have restated the reduction in sleep.

edits.anchor: As an aggregate, count-based counterpart to the per-window affinity

paras.text: In the S/Q/W analysis, *A*_{eff} = EPR/|*J*_{cycle}| was computed per fly and phase from the observed symbol-change counts (Eqs. 20, 22), for fly–phases with a cycle, finite entropy production and *J*_{cycle} ≠ 0. For a single cycle in a steady state, entropy production equals current times affinity, so *A*_{eff} estimates the cycle affinity; it agreed with the affinity of the fitted chain (Eq. 21) in every genotype. exp(*A*_{eff}) is the ratio of the probabilities of a forward and a backward turn of the cycle.
